rv.q: This mesmerising chronicle of an American dynasty sweeps past like one of those gigantic freight trains that roll across the Midwestern landscape.
Sam Mendes's magnificent 2018 staging of The Lehman Trilogy returns to London's West End with a terrific new cast...
A journey down the decades of raw, American capitalism, it’s a financial saga you can’t afford to miss.
It's really extraordinary stuff, and in parts better than its previous incarnations.
Mendes’s production is never less than riveting, and Massini’s play – and Ben Power’s adaption – often ferociously smart.
The production remains a tour de force, though. The new actors shine.
As pure, dizzying, audio-visual spectacle this is unrivalled — and still very much a show worth being able to say you've seen.
I still wish the play delivered a clear explanation of Lehmans' final implosion.
Its theatricality is utterly astonishing.
The Lehman Trilogy nonetheless remains majestically watchable.
Liquidate all your assets to buy a ticket.
This is a show not to be missed.
As it is, it is a unique and very special piece, a panoramic history that never loses sight of human detail and human cost.
The Lehman Trilogy is a miracle of charm. And a miracle of escapology.
Everything about the production – acting, set, projections, music, lighting, comic moments – made a perfect whole and, in this latest version, that sense of glorious theatrical unity remains.
No praise is too high for Sam Mendes’s production and an assemblage of design creatives that reveals Es Devlin’s sets, Jon Clark’s lighting, and Luke Halls’s video work as star turns all their own.
Their stories make for gripping theatre in Sam Mendes’ production that returns to London after a successful Broadway run.

Those expecting an exploration into the bank's role in the financial crisis will be disappointed; despite beginning and ending the show, we never get into the mechanics of the causes and the final crash does feel a little rushed.
The writing, direction and every production element come together seamlessly to create pure theatre magic at its finest.
This show has no right to be so much fun.

All three actors play various offspring, spouses and colleagues, and it's a tribute to Mendes' intelligent direction and the poetic restraint of Ben Power's adaptation, that the three hour plus running time never sags.
It’s a fascinating insight to the lives of the real-life Lehman Brothers and a fine study in acting, whether it also manages to be entertaining is up for debate.

cn.t: Mendes' epic production dazzles with its theatrical virtuosity and sweeping storytelling, as three actors masterfully chronicle 160 years of American capitalism through the Lehman family saga, though some find the financial crisis finale rushed.

vr.q: This is theater at its finest thanks to director Sam Mendes and his writers; if you haven't already seen it, don't miss this opportunity.
immediately knew upon leaving the theater that this was a great play a really great piece of theater and the performances are damn near perfect
